title: A component library a machine could read
standfirst: Expedia Group's components had drifted across iOS, Android and web. We rebuilt them against one written specification — the thing designers, engineers and language models all build from, instead of each interpreting a different source.

contribution.detail: Product Designer in the New Component Architecture pod, Expedia Group Design System

Components end to end: reading the generated plan, rebuilding in Figma from the ground up, and delivering the specification engineering built from. I also created the pod's designer onboarding as it grew.
Three designers and a principal, with Nathan Curtis contracted in for guidance. Engineering implemented from the spec.

problem.heading: The problem
problem.standfirst: Three platforms had built the same components independently for years. Nobody knew how far apart they had drifted until we asked a machine to read all three.
paras: A component was really four: one in the iOS repo, one in Android, one in web, and a Figma library matching none of them exactly. Each had its own props, arrangement rules and accumulated exceptions.

The fix was to stop treating any implementation as the source. One specification would define the component, and Figma, all three platforms and a language model would build from it — which only works if it is structured data rather than prose. A person can interpret a paragraph. Nothing else can build from one.

[NEEDS: the insight. Scraping three repos for one component produced a plan showing exactly how far apart they were — how many props existed on one platform and not the others, how many components were genuinely different rather than accidentally different. That number is both the problem statement and the baseline.]

process.heading: How a component got rebuilt
process.standfirst: A machine proposed each component by reading the code. A person decided what was actually right, and wrote the decision back in a form the machine could use.
paras: Every component started as a scrape. We read the iOS, Android and web repositories and generated a plan, which lived in GitHub beside the component: recommendations, configurations, elements, decisions, open questions, TODOs.

The plan was a proposal, not an instruction. I rebuilt each component against it — variables bound, slots attached, naming corrected, accessibility specified — and where the plan was wrong I overruled it and recorded why. Engineering implemented from the finished spec, with Code Connect holding Figma and code one to one.

That loop is the part worth taking forward. The machine did the reading, which no person was going to do across three codebases. The designer did the deciding — and the decision only counted once it was written somewhere the machine could read back.

[NEEDS: one example of the workflow changing because of what Q1 2026 testing showed. It ran with Expedia product designers, and with PMs and engineers who opted in. A reader asks specifically for a trade-off made because of testing, and that is the weakest part of this study.]
process.explorationsHeading: What the plan proposed, and what we overruled
process.explorationsIntro: These rejected paths are unusually well evidenced, because the alternative was not imagined. A machine proposed it from three real codebases, a person overruled it, and the reason went back into the record.

explorations.title: A vertical offset property, because React already had one
explorations.why: Rejected. Parents control arrangement outside a component, not the component itself. Carrying the prop forward would have moved a layout decision inside a boundary it does not belong in — on every platform, permanently.
explorations.imageAlt: The generated plan showing the vertical offset decision and its rationale

explorations.title: A dark frame variant for inverse surfaces
explorations.why: Rejected in favour of inverse tokens. A forced dark frame hardcodes a theme into a component; tokens let the surface decide, which is what made the system themable across brands.
explorations.imageAlt: The plan entry recommending inverse tokens over a dark frame

explorations.title: A maximum height, so message content crops after two lines
explorations.why: Left open, then rejected as a built-in constraint. Cropping is guidance, not something the component enforces. Building it in would have made the component wrong for every case that legitimately needed three lines.
explorations.imageAlt: The open question about message cropping and the recommendation against a max height

interface.heading: What shipped
interface.standfirst: One component, three platforms, each honouring its own conventions rather than one design relabelled three times.
interface.mediaAlt: The EGDS Dialog component set showing Web, iOS and Android variants of the same component
interface.mediaCaption: Platform is a variant axis on a single component. The iOS variant uses native alert conventions — centred heading, text action above a hairline — rather than inheriting the web treatment.
paras: Dialog shows the shape. Platform is a variant axis on one component set rather than three separate components, and its actions are a nested set covering one to three actions, two emphases and two arrangements.
[NEEDS: a second example, ideally harder than Dialog. Dialog is clean, and the reviewer is looking for complexity untangled — the component that fought back is the better story.]

impact.heading: Impact
impact.standfirst: The pod was made redundant before the architecture reached production. This is what was true when the work stopped.

In order of strength: anything measured in the Q1 2026 testing; time to produce a specification before and after the scraping workflow, which the tracking board's dates would show; the divergence the scrape found, which is a real number in the plans.]

We never instrumented it. The pod was made redundant before the architecture reached production, so the claim the whole project rested on — that the distance from idea to shipped code gets shorter — has a proof of concept behind it and no measurement.

That was avoidable, and it was my blind spot as much as anyone's. The baseline was measurable from the first scrape: we knew how long a component took to specify the old way and could have recorded it. Instrumenting at the start costs a day. Reconstructing it afterwards, as I am finding while writing this, is not possible at all.
[NEEDS: your own read, in your voice. A reader calls out self-awareness explicitly, so this is worth more than its length. Factual, free of grievance.]
